person who reads a troubling email and
immediately phones someone to talk it
through. The fix where you can protect
the first 30 minutes from conflict and
anxiety. Emotions aren't harmful, but
your body simply handles them better
once the morning surge has settled. And
if something is truly urgent, it will
still be urgent in an hour. Okay, that's
five. And now we've reached the one I
promised you at the start. Habit six,
brushing off morning symptoms. I want to
be careful here because the goal isn't
fear. It's telling apart what's common
from what's clinically significant. They
are not the same thing. Let me tell you
about a patient I'll call Margaret. She
was 74, a retired teacher, sharp and
organized, someone who tracked her sleep
and knew her cholesterol numbers. She
came in for a routine blood pressure
check. At the very end, almost as an
afterthought, she said, "I felt a bit
off in the mornings. There's a heaviness
across my shoulders when I get up and
sometimes my jaw feels tight. It goes
away in about 10 minutes. So, I figured
it was just how I sleep. I ordered
imaging that same week. She had a severe
blockage in a major artery. The kind
cardiologists call the widowmaker. The
heaviness, the jaw tightness, the way it
faded like clockwork. That was angina.
Not the dramatic chest pain from the
movies, but the quiet, easy to explain
version, which is especially common in
women. She had bypass surgery 6 weeks
later, and she's doing well today. But
notice what made the difference. She
mentioned it. Most people don't. They do
what the human brain does, which is find
a comfortable explanation and file it
away. Shoulder heaviness becomes, "I
need a new pillow." Jaw tightness
becomes, "I must be grinding my teeth."
Breathlessness on the stairs becomes,
"I'm just not as young as I was." Any of
those explanations might be true, but
these are the morning symptoms worth
taking seriously. Chest pressure,
tightness or heaviness after waking that
fades within 10 to 20 minutes, tightness
in the jaw, left arm, shoulder, or upper
back. New breathlessness on stairs or on
the walk to the kitchen. Palpitations,
meaning racing, fluttering or skipped
beats. Dizziness or lightadedness in the
first hour of the day. Deep unusual
fatigue from the moment you wake, unlike
ordinary tiredness. Frequent headaches
at the back of the head on waking, which
can be a clue to high blood pressure
overnight. No single item on that list
proves anything. But dismissing them
because they're familiar is the real
problem. Because familiar does not mean
safe. The fix. If any of these show up
repeatedly over weeks or months or even
once if it's significant, tell your
doctor. Don't frame it as a complaint.
Frame it as an observation. I've noticed
this in the mornings and I wanted to
mention it given my blood pressure
history. Then ask about a resting ECG, a
stress test, or a coronary calcium
score. Those aren't scary tests. They're
how your heart gets to say what it's
been trying to say. That's the full
list. But there's one more thing that
catches people who are trying hard to do
the right thing. A note on morning
exercise. If you exercise in the
morning, timing matters as much as type.
Picture a 71-year-old who walked 5 days
a week, had a low resting heart rate,
and ate well. He started feeling chest
discomfort, but only on morning walks,
never in the afternoon. The walks were
easy, so he brushed it off for weeks.
Testing showed serious narrowing in
several coronary arteries. His morning
walks, taken on a dehydrated body at the
peak of the hormone surge, sometimes in
cold air that tightens the vessels,
demanded more oxygen than his narrowed
arteries could deliver. Regular exercise
is one of the best things you can do for
your heart. But the same walk that's
easy at 2:00 p.m. can be a very
different demand at 6:30 a.m. So wait 30
to 45 minutes after waking, hydrate
first and warm up longer than you think
you need to with 8 to 10 minutes of
slow, easy movement before you pick up
the pace. And if you ever feel
discomfort or breathlessness,
specifically during morning activity,
mention it to your cardiologist. Now
that you know what to avoid, let's talk
about what to do instead. Morning heart
protection routine. Knowing what to
avoid only helps if you have something
to put in its place. This routine takes
about six to eight minutes, cost
nothing, and is designed to smooth the
morning transition instead of adding to
it. Step one, breathe before you move.
When you first wake, stay still for
about 90 seconds. Take five slow breaths
in through your nose for a count of four
and out through pursed lips for a count
of six. The long exhale activates the
calming branch of your nervous system.
The counterwe to the morning surge.
Small trials of slow breathing have
shown modest drops in blood pressure
with regular practice and it needs no
equipment. Step two, hydrate before you
stand. Keep 8 to 12 ounces of room
temperature water on your nightstand and
drink it while you're still sitting or
lying down. That starts correcting
overnight dehydration before your heart
is asked to work harder. If you take
morning medication, this is the moment.
With that water and if your doctor
agrees, a little food. Step three, sit
on the edge of the bed for 60 seconds.
Feet flat on the floor. Do a few slow
ankle pumps, pulling your toes toward
your shins, then pointing them down.
Your calf muscles work like a second
pump, pushing blood back toward your
heart and preventing the pooling that
causes dizziness when you stand too
fast. Step four, stand slowly and
stretch gently. Hold the nightstand or
headboard. Stand still for 5 to 10
seconds and make sure you feel steady
before you walk. Then spend about a
minute on easy movement with arms
overhead, gentle side bends,
[clears throat]
and slow neck turns. This wakes up your
circulation gradually and gives your
pressure sensing system time to catch
up. Step five, protect the first 20
minutes. No phone, no news, no
arguments, water, gentle movement, and a
protein-based breakfast. This one
guardrail covers habits 1, 2, and five
all at once. Now, a routine works even
better when your doctor is on the same
page. Five questions for your next
appointment. These turn a routine
check-in into a real conversation based
on my readings and history. Do I have
morning hypertension? And is my
treatment targeting that early window?
Has my medication timing ever been
reviewed against my highest risk time of
day? Is there a more protective
schedule? Do I show signs of insulin
resistance or high fasting glucose that
might be adding to my morning risk? What
should I change at breakfast? Are there
symptoms I may be normalizing like
morning headaches, palpitations, or
unusual fatigue that you'd like me to
track and report? Given my heart health,
what's the safest way to start morning
exercise? And would any testing help set
the right intensity? A doctor who cares
about your long-term heart health will
welcome every one of these. But knowing
is one thing and doing is another. So,
let me make it easy. The Here's your
challenge and it's gradual on purpose.
Tomorrow, just two changes, 90 seconds
of slow breathing and a glass of water
before anything else, before coffee and
before your phone. Days 1 to three. If
you have a home blood pressure monitor,
take a reading within 15 minutes of
waking, before coffee, and before
activity, and write it down. No monitor,
rate from 1 to 10 how steady, clear, and
energized you feel in the first half
hour. Day 10, add the 60-second sit on
the edge of the bed with ankle pumps.
Day 18, add the 20 minute phonefree,
conflict-free buffer. Day 25, add a
proteinbased breakfast within an hour of
waking. Day 30, measure again or rate
your energy and steadiness again and
compare. Many people who follow a
gradual routine like this notice
steadier mornings, less dizziness, and a
calmer start to the day. Nothing
dramatic changed. Your heart is just no
longer being asked to handle its
toughest transition of the day while
carrying extra avoidable loads. The
morning window isn't a theory. It's
biology. And it's happening in your body
every day whether you notice or not.
What changes when you understand it
isn't the biology. It's how you treat
that first hour. So, let's recap. You
know the triple pressure window. You
know the six habits that add load to it.
You have a routine that takes a few
minutes and you have five questions that
will lift your next appointment above
the usual. No prescription, no
equipment, no life overhaul, just small
changes to an hour you're already
living. And remember Margaret, her jaw
tightness went away every single
morning. And that's exactly what made it
so easy to ignore. The heart doesn't
always shout. Sometimes it whispers. And
mornings are when that whisper is
loudest. Now you know what to listen
for. If this helped, hit like,
subscribe, and share it with someone
whose heart and mourns you care about.
And before you go, there's a second half
to this story. The risk doesn't begin
when you wake up. It can begin while
you're still asleep. There's a video
about a sleeping position that may raise
stroke risk overnight, and it's on your
screen right now. Take care of
yourselves and I'll see you

Don’t Skip These 5 Vegetables for Your Kidneys Health Over 50? (A Kidney Doctor Explains)

After 50, your food choices can play an important role in kidney health.
Discover 5 nutritious vegetables: zucchini, red bell peppers, onions, cabbage, and cauliflower.
Learn simple ways to add these vegetables to your diet while supporting healthy kidneys naturally.

subtitles.plaintext:
If you're over 50, and your plate is
missing these five vegetables, your
kidneys may be working overtime, and you
wouldn't feel a thing. Most seniors hear
the same two instructions: eat less
salt, drink more water. Good advice, but
it's only half the picture. What you add
to your plate can protect your kidneys
just as much as what you remove. Maybe
you felt puffy lately. Maybe your energy
dips by mid-afternoon, or your thinking
feels cloudy. You might blame age, but
sometimes it's your kidneys quietly
asking for help. Your kidneys filter
your blood around the clock, and they're
tougher than you'd think, but they're
also sensitive to inflammation, to
oxidative stress, and to too much of
certain minerals. And many senior diets
are short on the very vegetables that
ease that pressure. The good news? You
don't need pricey superfoods or
complicated recipes. You need the right
everyday vegetables prepared the right
way. In this video, we'll count down
five vegetables that support kidney
health after 50. They're affordable,
easy to find, and gentle on aging
digestion. And number two, most people
walk right past it at the grocery store,
and it might be the one you've
overlooked the longest. Stay with me.
Before we start, tell me in the comments
how old you are, and where you're
watching from. I love reading them. If
this video helps you, a quick like and a
subscribe means a lot, and it helps us
reach more people over 50. Number five,
zucchini. Let's start with a vegetable
that's mild, soft, and wonderfully easy
to eat, zucchini. Because it's so plain,
many people treat it as filler. That's a
mistake. Zucchini is about 95% water,
which makes it hydrating and light on
your system. It's naturally very low in
sodium and phosphorus, and it has a
moderate amount of potassium. Half a cup
of cooked zucchini has roughly 200 mg,
so a small portion fits nicely into most
kidney-conscious meals. It also brings
vitamin C, which helps your body fight
oxidative stress, and small amounts of B
vitamins that your cells use for energy.
It's gentle fiber keeps digestion moving
without irritation, and that matters
because a sluggish gut can add to the
body's overall burden. Picture Emma, a
71-year-old who felt worn out and
stopped cooking because everything
seemed like too much work. Her
granddaughter suggested one easy habit,
sauté sliced zucchini in a little olive
oil with fresh herbs every evening. It
took 5 minutes. Within a month, Emma
told us she felt lighter, less bloated,
and proud to be cooking again. If
chewing is hard, steam it until tender.
Short on time? Grate it into scrambled
eggs or soup. Zucchini won't win any
popularity contests, but it quietly does
its job. Next, a colorful vegetable
that's loaded with protective power.
Number four, red bell peppers. Bright,
sweet, and a smart swap for salty
seasonings. Here's something many people
don't realize. Red peppers are among the
richest vegetable sources of vitamin C,
and they also contain vitamin A and
antioxidants like lycopene. Why does
that matter for your kidneys? Because
oxidative stress, the slow wear and tear
caused by unstable molecules called free
radicals, is one of the key drivers of
kidney decline. Antioxidants help calm
it down. On the numbers, half a cup of
chopped red pepper has around 130 mg of
potassium, very little phosphorus, and
almost no sodium. That's why renal
dietitians often recommend peppers as a
flavor booster. And that's the hidden
gift. When you cut back on salt, food
can taste flat. Red pepper adds
sweetness, color, and a little crunch,
so you won't miss the shaker. Eat them
raw with hummus, roast them until soft
and smoky, or slice them into stir-fries
and omelets.
If you'd rather avoid the skin, roasted
peppers peel easily and digest well.
Colorful food is also more appealing,
and eating well is easier when your
plate looks inviting. Let's keep going.
Number three is a kitchen staple you
probably use every week without
realizing how much it does. Number
three, onions. Onions are in everything,
but we You think of them as medicine.
They contain a flavonoid called
quercetin, an antioxidant studied for
its ability to calm inflammation and
support healthy blood pressure. And
blood pressure is critical because high
pressure damages the tiny filters inside
your kidneys over time. Half a cup of
chopped onion is low in sodium and
phosphorus with only around 120 mg of
potassium. That makes it a perfect
flavor base. And here's the real kidney
benefit. Onions let you build deep
savory taste without salt.
Sauté them slowly until golden and they
become naturally sweet and rich. Add
garlic and herbs and you've replaced a
seasoning packet full of sodium with
something your kidneys will actually
appreciate. Worried about harsh
digestion? Cook them well. Slow-cooked
onions are much gentler than raw ones.
Try them in soups, with roasted
vegetables, or folded into scrambled
eggs. Think of onions as the foundation.
Everything else you cook gets better and
healthier because of them.
Now we're getting to the surprising one.
Number two, cabbage. This is the one I
said most seniors ignore and I'd bet
it's been years since you put it on your
plate. Cabbage looks plain. It sits at
the bottom of the produce aisle and
costs next to nothing. But for aging
kidneys, it's remarkable. Start with the
numbers. Half a cup of cooked cabbage
has around 60 mg of potassium, a handful
of milligrams of phosphorus, and very
little sodium. That's one of the lowest
mineral loads of any vegetable, which is
why it's considered so safe for people
watching their kidney numbers. But
cabbage goes beyond safe. It's a
cruciferous vegetable packed with plant
compounds like glucosinolates and
anthocyanins in the red variety.
These help your body neutralize
inflammation and protect delicate tissue
from oxidative damage.
Cabbage also provides vitamin K for bone
strength. And that's important after 60
because struggling kidneys can disrupt
calcium balance. And the fiber?
It helps regulate blood sugar and
cholesterol, two things that strain your
blood vessels. And your kidneys depend
on healthy blood vessels. Now, if raw
cabbage upsets your stomach, cook it.
Simmered in soup, sauteed with a little
olive oil, or braised until silky, it
becomes tender and mild. Red and green
both work, and a head lasts for weeks in
your fridge. For the price of a cup of
coffee, you get a week of kidney
support. That's why it earned spot and
why ignoring it has been a costly
oversight. Up next, the vegetable that
tops our list. It's soft, versatile, and
a lifesaver for anyone missing potatoes.
Number one, cauliflower. If I could
recommend just one vegetable to a senior
who wants to protect their kidneys, this
would be it. Half a cup of cooked
cauliflower contains only about 88 mg of
potassium and 20 mg of phosphorus with
hardly any sodium. When your kidneys
slow down, they struggle to clear
potassium and phosphorus. Too much can
cause weakness, fatigue, irregular
heartbeat, and weaker bones over time.
Cauliflower gives you nutrition without
that risk. It also delivers vitamin C,
folate, vitamin K, and fiber. Plus,
those same protective cruciferous
compounds that help reduce inflammation
and support your body's natural cleanup
systems. But, here's what makes it
number one. It replaces foods you may
have been told to avoid. Missing mashed
potatoes? Steam cauliflower until very
soft, mash it with olive oil and a
little garlic, and you'll have creamy
comfort food without the potassium
spike.
Want something lighter? Try cauliflower
rice. Or roast florets until golden and
nutty. It's mild flavor works with
nearly anything, and its soft texture is
easy on sensitive stomachs. It's
affordable, available year-round, and
once you try it, surprisingly easy to
love. Smart tips. Now that you know the
five, here's how to get the most from
them. One, rotate. Variety protects you.
Eating a wide range of vegetables
spreads out minerals and keeps your diet
balanced. Two, cook for comfort. Gentle
steaming, roasting, or simmering softens
fibers and makes eating easier. Three,
watch portions. Even kidney-friendly
vegetables contain potassium. If you're
on a restricted plan, stick to about
half a cup cooked per serving and ask
your dietitian what's right for you.
Four, add healthy fat. A drizzle of
olive oil helps your body absorb
fat-soluble vitamins like A and K. Five,
season smartly. Skip salty packets and
sauces. Use herbs, lemon, garlic, and
pepper instead. Six, prep ahead. Wash
and chop on Sunday so healthy choices
are easy all week. Seven, listen to your
body.
If a food leaves you bloated or tired,
adjust the portion or the cooking method
and tell your doctor. Let's recap.
Zucchini, light and hydrating.
Red peppers, rich in antioxidants.
Onions, the flavor base that replaces
salt.
Cabbage, the overlooked bargain at
number two.
And cauliflower, our number one, the
kidney-friendly answer to potatoes.
Remember Emma? She didn't overhaul her
life. She added one simple vegetable
dish each evening and it changed how she
felt. You can do the same. So, here's
your challenge. Pick one vegetable from
this list and add it to a meal this
week. Just one. Small steps become
habits and habits protect your health.
Tell me in the comments which one you're
starting with. Your answer might inspire
someone else. A quick note. This video
is for education, not medical advice. If
you have kidney disease, talk with your
doctor or dietitian about portions,
especially for potassium. Thanks for
watching. Stay curious, stay consistent,
and take care of those kidneys.

5 Pills You’re Taking After 60 Could Be Raising Heart Attack & Stroke Risk | Cardiologist Warns

Are common medications affecting your heart health after 60? In this video, we explore 5 medication categories that may impact blood pressure, heart rhythm, electrolyte balance, blood sugar, and cardiovascular health in older adults—including diphenhydramine sleep aids, diuretics, statins, decongestants, and sulfonylurea diabetes medications.

You’ll discover why over-the-counter sleep aids containing diphenhydramine may cause anticholinergic and cardiovascular effects, how diuretics can influence potassium and magnesium levels, what research suggests about statins and CoQ10, why pseudoephedrine may increase blood pressure and heart rate, and how sulfonylurea-related low blood sugar can put extra stress on the cardiovascular system.

This video also covers medication safety for seniors, potential drug interactions, electrolyte monitoring, hypoglycemia, high blood pressure, irregular heart rhythms, cardiovascular risks, and medication reviews. Most importantly, this is not advice to stop any prescribed medication—the final section highlights practical questions you can discuss with your doctor or pharmacist.

If you’re over 60, take several prescription or over-the-counter medications, or live with heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, or other cardiovascular risk factors, this medication-awareness guide can help you prepare for a safer, more informed medication review.

If you are over 60 and swallow even a
single pill each day, I'd ask you to
stick with me for the next few minutes.
What I'm about to explain is something
most people never hear in a doctor's
office. That's not because doctors are
keeping secrets. A standard 10-minute
appointment just doesn't leave space for
a conversation like this one. People do
everything correctly. They take each
pill on schedule, refill every
prescription on time, and follow every
instruction they're given. And still,
their cardiovascular system slowly wears
down. Sometimes because of the very
medication sitting in their cabinet at
this moment. I'm not talking about rare
or exotic drugs. I'm talking about pills
that millions of Americans over 60 take
daily with little real understanding of
what those pills do to the heart and
blood vessels across months and years of
nonstop use. This video covers five of
them. By the time we reach number one, I
expect the way you see your medicine
cabinet to be changed for good. My name
is Dr. Dennis. My background is
cardiovascular health research with a
particular on how prescription and
over-the-counter medications interact
with the aging heart and blood vessels.
That meeting point, where everyday pills
encounter an aging body, is where the
most overlooked dangers hide. And
uncovering them is exactly why this
channel exists. Several years into my
research, I encountered a case that
redirected everything for me. Lucas Paul
was 67, a healthy weight, a non-smoker
who walked his dog every evening. For 4
years, he took every medication
faithfully and never missed a dose. Then
one Sunday afternoon, he collapsed in
his kitchen having gone into a dangerous
cardiac arrhythmia that can be fatal
within minutes without treatment. He
survived. But when I sat down and went
through his complete medication history,
including dosages, combinations, and the
over-the-counter products he'd added
along the way, one thing became
unmistakably clear. Lucas wasn't
unlucky. Lucas was uninformed. That
difference reshaped everything I do. So,
let's get into the five. We'll count
down from five to one building toward
the category that worries me most.
Before we go any further, drop a number
in the comments right now. How many
pills, prescription or over-the-counter,
do you or someone you love take every
day? Just a number. I'd like to see it.
And before we begin, everything in this
video is for educational purposes only.
It does not replace advice from your own
physician who knows your complete
medical history. Number five, OTC sleep
aids, diphenhydramine.
Number five is something millions of
seniors pick up without a second
thought, the over-the-counter sleep aid.
Specifically, products that contain an
ingredient called diphenhydramine.
You'll know them as Benadryl, ZzzQuil,
and Unisom. No prescription needed,
shelved right beside the vitamins.
Because they're so easy to get, most
people assume they're harmless. Here's
the pharmacology the label never
explains. Diphenhydramine belongs to a
class of compounds called
anticholinergics.
They work by blocking a chemical
messenger in the nervous system called
acetylcholine. When acetylcholine
activity is suppressed in the heart, it
interferes with the heart's electrical
signaling and can trigger a racing
pulse, palpitations, and in some cases
abnormal rhythms. An expert review in
the Journal of Clinical Medicine reports
that the cardiovascular side effects of
diphenhydramine include tachycardia, ECG
abnormalities, and arrhythmias, and that
use in the elderly is specifically
discouraged because the risk rises with
repeated exposure. A large
population-based cohort study published
in 2025 found a dose-response
relationship between cumulative
anticholinergic drug burden and
cardiovascular events in older adults,
with the highest exposure group showing
significantly higher rates of heart
failure and arrhythmias. The more of
these drugs a person took, the higher
the risk climbed. Here's why this
matters so much after 60.
In a younger adult, a temporary
arrhythmia from a sleep aid is
uncomfortable. In someone whose heart is
already coping with the natural changes
of aging, such as reduced flexibility,
slower recovery, and less electrical
reserve, the same disruption carries far
greater consequences. I reviewed the
case of a 71-year-old retired librarian
who spent nearly a year being evaluated
for nighttime palpitations that woke her
three or four times a week. Her tests
came back fine and no clear diagnosis
emerged. When a thorough medication
review was finally done, covering
everything she took without a
prescription, she mentioned almost as an
afterthought that she took Benadryl most
nights to fall asleep. She'd done that
for 14 months. Once it was stopped under
medical supervision, her palpitations
cleared up within 3 weeks. 14 months of
needless cardiac stress from something
she picked up in the cold medicine
aisle. If you use any OTC sleep aid
regularly, check the active ingredient
on the label tonight. Look for
diphenhydramine and write it down. We'll
talk about what to do with that list at

If You Sleep Like This After 60, Watch Before Tonight (Cardiologist Warns About Stroke Risk)


Could your sleeping position affect stroke risk, blood pressure, circulation, and brain health overnight?
In this video, we explore 5 nighttime habits and sleep positions that may influence cardiovascular and brain health in older adults.
You’ll learn about sleep apnea, oxygen levels, dehydration, blood pressure, circulation, and the brain’s overnight waste-clearing system.
Most importantly, you’ll discover practical sleep habits and warning signs that may help support better sleep, heart health, and overnight brain health.

airway collapse in sleep disordered
breathing. You get an unstable airway,
repeated oxygen drops, repeated
adrenaline surges, and repeated blood
pressure spikes every night. The
American Academy of Sleep Medicine has
published data connecting obstructive
sleep apnea, disrupted overnight blood
pressure, and stroke. The findings
aren't subtle. A 20-year follow-up study
reported that people with moderate to
severe obstructive sleep apnea were
nearly four times more likely to have a
stroke than those without it,
independent of weight, blood pressure,
and smoking. Here's the part that haunts
me as a clinician. Most adults who snore
heavily have never been formally
evaluated. They've been told they snore.
Their partner complains. They feel tired
in the morning. But, they've never had a
sleep study, and they don't realize
those sounds from their throat are the
outward sign of a physiological crisis
repeating inside their cardiovascular
system. If you snore, or your partner
has ever said you stop breathing in your
sleep, please make that call this week.

inexpensive. And what it reveals could
be the most important health discovery
of your decade. What to do instead?
Position one, left side sleeping set up
properly. Left side sleeping isn't just
a nicer choice. There's specific
physiology behind why it protects your
brain and heart at once. Your heart sits
slightly left of center. On your left
side, gravity assists venous return, so
blood flows from your lower body back
toward the right atrium with less
resistance, and your heart does less
work per beat across 8 hours.
That difference in cardiac workload adds
up. What makes it truly remarkable for
older adults is the glymphatic pathway.
Your brain's dedicated overnight waste
removal network. During deep sleep,
cerebrospinal fluid is driven through
channels around your brain's blood
vessels and flushes out metabolic
debris, including amyloid beta and tau
proteins, the same ones that accumulate
in Alzheimer's disease.
A 2015 study in the Journal of
Neuroscience by researchers at Stony
Brook University and the University of
Rochester found that glymphatic
transport was most efficient in the
lateral or side position compared with
lying on the back or stomach. That work
was done in rodents with human evidence
now building a similar picture. What the
data shows is that side sleeping as a
category clears brain waste better than
back or stomach sleeping. Every night in
a less ideal position is a night your
brain's cleaning crew runs at reduced
capacity and the proteins it misses
don't vanish. They accumulate over years
and decades. Practically, here's how to
set it up. Put a full-length body pillow
in front of you so you don't roll
forward and compress your chest. Place a
pillow between your knees to keep your
hips aligned and spare your lower back.
Keep your bottom shoulder slightly
forward rather than trapped under your
weight.
Expect to roll over during the night.
That's normal, not failure. The aim is
to spend most of your sleep in this
position, not to be perfect. Position
two, slightly elevated back sleeping. If
side sleeping is impractical because of
shoulder arthritis, hip pain, or other
limits, slightly elevated back sleeping
is a viable, evidence-supported
alternative. The key word is elevated,
not flat. Use a firm foam wedge that
lifts your entire upper torso, not just
your head, to roughly 15 to 20°. That
incline helps venous return from your
lower body, lowers venous pressure
inside the skull, and in many cases
reduces apnea events compared with lying
flat. Put a small pillow or rolled towel
under your knees to protect your lower
back curve. If you have diagnosed
moderate to severe sleep apnea, back
sleeping may not be enough even with
elevation and the left side remains
safer. But for those managing mild
snoring, borderline blood pressure, and
early circulation concerns, this
position offers real protection without
a complete habit overhaul.

gulp water right before bed. Hydrate
well through the afternoon and taper off
by early evening. Try to finish your
main fluid intake by 7:00 p.m. Then keep

on your nightstand and drink it in the
morning before you stand up. That modest
rehydration before your first upright
movement helps offset the morning rise
in blood thickness and softens your
morning cardiovascular surge. Your sleep
environment, even the best position
works inside an environment that either
supports or sabotages your recovery.
Temperature, it matters more than most
people think. Your core temperature has
to drop start the deep sleep stages
where real cardiovascular recovery
happens. A room between 64 and 67° F
lets that drop happen efficiently. A
warm room keeps you cycling through
lighter sleep. Your heart rate stays up.
Your blood pressure doesn't fall as it
should, and you wake feeling like you
never rested. Screens, screen use after
9:00 p.m. suppresses melatonin through
blue light, delaying deep sleep and with
it the glymphatic flush and blood
pressure dip your brain and vessels
need. Noise, even sounds that never
fully wake you trigger brief sympathetic
responses. Your heart rate jumps and
cortisol pulses into your bloodstream. A
steady sound environment, whether from a
white noise machine or good ear plugs,
removes those small stressors from your
overnight picture. Tracking, you can
also see what your body is doing
overnight without complicated gear. An
overnight pulse oximeter, a simple
fingertip clip, records your blood
oxygen through the night. If it
regularly falls below 92%, that's
clinically significant and worth showing
your doctor. A simple journal of morning
symptoms, such as headaches, dizziness
on standing, tingling in hands or feet,
or mental fog can reveal patterns a
quarterly blood draw never will. Bring
dates and details to your doctor and
you'll get a real diagnostic
conversation. These tools don't replace
medical care. They make it more
effective. Why your doctor hasn't told
you this? Sleep positioning has no
billing code. There's no drug for it, no
lab value, no scan that captures what
your body does during the 8 hours your
doctor never sees. A 15-minute visit
centered on prescriptions and blood work
leaves no room for a talk about pillow
height or which side you sleep on. That
doesn't make this speculative. The
research on glymphatic function,
positional stroke risk, the morning
surge, and sleep apnea's cardiovascular
effects is well-established. It just
isn't reaching routine practice fast
enough. So, learning it now puts you
ahead of the curve. Closing, pick one
thing from today, just one. Maybe you'll
move to your left side tonight with a
body pillow. Maybe you'll call your
doctor this week to ask about a sleep
study. Maybe you'll put a small glass of
water by the bed and turn off screens 45
minutes earlier. One change, 7 days.
Notice how you feel each morning. Tell
me in the comments which change you're
starting with. Your answer might help
someone else in this audience recognize
a pattern they've been dismissing for
years. And if someone in your life is
over 60, manages blood pressure, snores
loudly, or keeps waking with headaches
they can't explain, share this video
with them. That conversation may matter
more than you realize. If you aren't
subscribed, do it now. And here's why
this week in particular matters.
Next week, I'm releasing a video on five
minerals that cardiovascular research
has directly tied to lower overnight
stroke risk. These aren't
blogger-promoted supplements. They're
specific nutrients with documented
mechanisms found mostly in ordinary
groceries.
But there are two details most people
get wrong. When to take them and one
common pairing that actually cancels out
the benefit.

#seniorhealth #Nocturia #NighttimeUrination #Urology #BladderHealth 
Urologist Reveals: How to Drink Water to Avoid Getting Up at Night Over 60!

Waking up to urinate once or twice may seem normal after 50, but frequent nighttime bathroom trips (nocturia) can disrupt sleep, raise fall risk, and affect your health. In this video, Dr. Dinnes explains how to time your water intake to reduce nighttime trips and why simply “drinking less water at night” may not fix the problem.

Discover the 5-part Circadian Hydration Method for adults over 50: drink more water earlier, gradually taper fluids in the afternoon, manage caffeine and alcohol timing, reduce evening sodium, and follow a simple pre-sleep drainage routine with leg elevation, a short walk, and fully emptying your bladder.

The video also covers ADH and aging, kidney function, fluid buildup in the legs, bladder sensitivity, prostate enlargement, diabetes, sleep apnea, hydration timing, caffeine, alcohol, sodium, and nighttime urination, plus other possible contributing health factors too.

You’ll get a practical morning-to-bedtime hydration schedule and learn when ongoing nocturia may require a conversation with your doctor.

🚃Research References:
Ogawa et al. — Potassium intake and kidney output, Am J Kidney Diseases, 2018
van Kerrebroeck P et al. — Nocturia treatment and leg elevation, BJU International, 2002
Weiss JP, Blaivas JG — Nocturia classification and causes, J Urology, 2000
Epstein M — Alcohol and ADH suppression, Alcohol Health Research World, 1997
Umlauf MG, Chasens ER — Sleep apnea and nocturia, Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2003

9 mistakes People Make Before Blood Tests and how to avoid it! | Doctor Explain

Proper blood test preparation is essential for accurate results. Learn the 9 mistakes to avoid before your next appointment. Whether you are managing a chronic condition or attending routine checkups, your actions in the days leading up to your appointment directly affect your lab results. Many patients do not realize that everyday habits can interfere with the data your doctor relies on to make decisions about your care. For example, taking certain biotin supplements can cause falsely low troponin readings, which may complicate your medical testing.

This guide covers exactly what you should avoid, from a few days out to the morning of your draw. Following these steps helps ensure that the information your healthcare provider receives is accurate and actionable. By being aware of these common pitfalls, you can feel more confident and prepared for your next visit.

You open your lab portal a few days
after your blood draw and your stomach
drops.
Your triglycerides are high, your kidney
number is flagged, your thyroid looks
strange. So, you worry, you book another
test, and maybe you get sent to a
specialist, but sometimes the problem
was never inside your body. It was
something you did in the hours or days
before the needle ever touched your arm.
I'm Dr. Dennis and I see this more often
than you'd think. A blood test is a
snapshot of one moment in time and the
smallest habits can change what that
snapshot shows. A mint in the car, a
hard morning workout, a vitamin you've
taken for years without a second
thought. Any of them can nudge a number
just far enough to cause confusion,
extra costs, and a repeat visit. Today,
I'm going to walk you through nine
hidden mistakes people make before blood
draw, explain what each one can do to
your results, and tell you exactly what
to do instead. I'll also point out a few
popular rules you can relax about. And
stay until mistake number seven because
it involves a supplement millions of
people take for their hair and nails and
it can fool some very important tests.
Before we start, two questions because I
read every comment. When was your last
blood test and did you do anything that
morning like coffee, a workout, or a
vitamin that you now suspect changed
your numbers? Much of what circulates as
blood test advice is outdated, overly
cautious, or flat wrong and I'd like to
set the record straight one mistake at a
time. Let's begin with the mistake I see
most often. Mistake number one is
breaking your fast without realizing you
did it. Here's how it usually goes.
Someone is told to fast, so they skip
breakfast and feel proud of themselves.
Then, on the drive to the lab, they sip
a little coffee, chew a piece of gum, or
pop a breath mint because surely that
count. But when a test requires fasting,
it does count. The safest rule is water
only, no coffee even black, no tea, no
juice, no soda, no mints. Why does this
matter? Because food and drink change
your blood in real time. Sugar raises
your glucose and insulin. Fat from a
recent meal can raise your
triglycerides, and since many labs
calculate your LDL cholesterol using
triglycerides, that number can drift,
too. Even your creatinine, the marker we
use to judge how your kidneys are
filtering, can move a little after
eating. Now, here's the nuance so you
don't worry more than you need to. Not
every test requires fasting. A
hemoglobin A1C, which reflects your
average blood sugar over about 3 months,
usually doesn't. And many labs now
accept non-fasting cholesterol panels
because research shows they're often
just as useful. So, don't follow what
your neighbor did. And don't follow what
you were told 10 years ago. Follow the
instructions given for your test. And if
you slip and eat something, tell the
person drawing your blood. 10 seconds of
honesty can save you an entire second
trip. Mistake number two is the opposite
error, fasting for far too long. Some
people hear 8 to 12 hours and decide
that more must be better. So, they show
up having eaten nothing for 16, 18, even
24 hours.
But once your body runs out of quick
fuel, it starts tapping into its own
reserves. That's a normal survival
process, but it changes your blood
chemistry. Different fats and byproducts
appear, and the lab ends up measuring a
body that's searching for energy instead
of a body at rest. It can also be
unsafe. If you take insulin or certain
diabetes medications, going too long
without food can drop your blood sugar.
That can mean shakiness, sweating,
dizziness, and in some cases fainting
right there in the chair.
So, don't treat fasting like a contest.
Aim for the window you were given, not
an extreme one. A longer fast does not
give you a more accurate result. It
gives you a different one. Quick pause.
If this video is already changing how
you think about your next blood draw,
tap the like button so more people can
find it. And if you're not subscribed
yet, now is a great time because next
I'm covering a mistake that sounds like
it contradicts fasting and it trips up a
lot of people. Mistake number three is
not drinking enough water. Some people
hear the word fasting and assume it
means nothing at all water included. But
routine fasting tests, plain water is
allowed and it actually helps. When
you're dehydrated, your blood becomes
more concentrated.
That can push up your BUN, which stands
for blood urea nitrogen, and your
creatinine.
Because creatinine is used to calculate
your estimated glomerular filtration
rate or EGFR,
your kidney score can look worse than it
really is.
Let me be careful here. A high
creatinine does not automatically mean
you were dehydrated. There are plenty of
reasons it can rise, including real
kidney disease. But if you arrived at
the lab after hardly drinking anything
all day, your doctor should know that
when interpreting the result. There's
also a very practical benefit.
Dehydrated veins are smaller and harder
to find, which can mean more pokes, more
bruising, and a longer morning for
everyone. So drink your normal amount of
water the day before and have a glass or
two the morning of your test unless
you've been told otherwise. But don't
guzzle a gallon to try to make your
numbers look better.
And if you have advanced kidney disease,
heart failure, or you're on dialysis
with a fluid limit, follow the limit
your care team gave you. The goal is an
accurate picture of your health, not a
staged one.
Mistake number four is guessing about
your medications. And people guess in
two opposite directions. Some assume
fasting means skipping every pill they
own. Others take everything as usual,
even when one of their medications needs
special timing. Neither habit is
automatically safe. Think about insulin.
If you take it and then don't eat, your
blood sugar can crash. Now, think about
blood pressure medication or seizure
medication. If you skip those, even for
a day, your blood pressure can spike or
your protection against seizures can
weaken. And thyroid medication is a good
example of how specific this can get.
For certain thyroid measurements, the
timing of your pill relative to the
blood draw can matter. But, that doesn't
mean everyone should skip it. The right
answer depends on what is being measured
and why. So, here is the one question to
ask before any blood test. Should I take
my regular medications before this test
or wait until afterward? Ask the
clinician who prescribes them, not the
person drawing your blood. And while
you're at it, tell your doctor about
everything you use. I mean, everything.
Hormone treatments, weight loss
injections, medications from a wellness
clinic, even things you got from a
friend. I once cared for a man whose red
blood cell count came back high. His
doctor was seriously considering a
referral to a blood specialist to look
for a bone marrow disorder. But, he
hadn't mentioned that he was on
testosterone pellets. And testosterone
is well-known for raising red blood cell
counts. One sentence at the right moment
could have saved him weeks of worry.
That's how much the full story matters.
Mistake number five is working out hard
right before your blood draw. Exercise
feels like the healthiest thing in the
world, and it is. But, intense exercise
causes tiny amounts of muscle breakdown,
and that releases enzymes into your
bloodstream. Creatine kinase or CK can
jump. AST, which many people call a
liver enzyme, can rise, too, because it
also lives in your muscles. Your
creatinine, your blood sugar, and even
your white blood cell count can shift
for a while afterward. The problem is
that these changes can look a lot like
real muscle injury or liver trouble.
That can lead to repeat testing,
unnecessary stress, and sometimes a
referral to a specialist you never
needed. And if your doctor is
specifically checking CK or
investigating unexplained liver or
muscle enzymes, the effect matters even
more. Now, a calm walk around the block
is not going to ruin your results. We're
talking about heavy lifting, long runs,
and hard interval training. So, skip the
strenuous stuff for about 24 hours
before your draw, and ask whether you
need a longer break if your doctor is
looking at muscle or liver markers. Then
go right back to your routine afterward.
This is a pause, not a punishment.
Mistake number six is the dinner and
drinks the night before. Plenty of
people believe that once they've fasted
for 8 or 12 hours, whatever they ate
before, that no longer matters. But, it
can. A big fatty meal can keep your
triglycerides elevated for many hours,
well into the next morning. A large
portion of cooked meat can temporarily
raise your creatinine, so your kidney
number looks mildly off because of a
steak and not a problem.
And some tests have their own food
rules. One example is a test called
5-HIAA,
where you may be asked to avoid bananas,
avocados, pineapple, walnuts, and
eggplant. Perfectly healthy foods, but
they contain a compound the test is
hunting for. Alcohol is the other big
player, and it clears more slowly than
most people expect. A couple of drinks
the night before can raise your
triglycerides, shift your liver enzymes,
and change your blood sugar. And if you
just came back from a vacation, a
wedding weekend, or a heavy week of
social events, that's not the best time
to check your liver or your cholesterol,
unless your doctor wants to see exactly
that. So, eat normally the day before,
skip the giant late-night feast, and
avoid alcohol for at least a full day,
longer if your doctor recommends it.
Now, here's the one I promised. Mistake
number seven is forgetting about
supplements, especially biotin. Biotin,
also called vitamin B7, is in most hair,
skin, and nail products. And let me
clear up a common myth first. Biotin
does not harm your thyroid, and it does
not harm your heart. The problem is that
it can interfere with how certain lab
tests read your blood. Many modern tests
work by using a kind of molecular hook
to catch the substance they're
measuring. If there's too much biotin in
your sample, it can get in the way of
that process. Depending on how the test
is built, a thyroid result can look
higher or lower than the truth. That can
lead a doctor to think a thyroid is
overactive, or that a medication dose is
too high, when neither is true. Even
more concerning, some troponin tests,
which help detect a heart attack, can
produce falsely low results when biotin
is present.
That is the kind of error nobody wants.
Now, not every supplement contains
enough biotin to cause interference,
and not every test is affected. The
dose, how recently you took it, how well
your kidneys work, and the lab's method
all play a role. That's why I don't tell
everyone to stop every supplement for
days. Instead, bring the bottle, or
write down the exact dose, and ask
whether you should pause it before this
particular test. And don't forget
multivitamins, herbal products, and
protein powders. If you take it
regularly, your care team should know
about it. Mistake number eight is
getting tested at the wrong time of day,
or after a terrible night of sleep. Your
body runs on a clock, and many of your
hormones follow it. Cortisol, your main
stress hormone, is highest in the early
morning, around 6:00 to 8:00, and falls
to its lowest point near midnight. Test
it any afternoon, and it can look low
even in someone perfectly healthy.
Testosterone also peaks early and drops
as the day goes on. So, a late test can
make normal levels look low. Iron moves
around during the day as well, and the
reference ranges your results are
compared against were largely built from
morning blood draws, which is why an
early appointment isn't just a
tradition. It keeps the comparison fair.
Sleep matters, too. If you stayed up all
night working or traveling and then went
straight to the lab, your morning
cortisol and testosterone can come back
off. And here's a twist. If your doctor
suspects too much cortisol, the test may
actually be done at midnight using a
saliva sample because that's when
cortisol should be at its lowest. So,
when your doctor gives you a time,
follow it and try to sleep well the
night before.
Mistake number nine is bad timing around
your life and your care. This one has
three parts. First, testing during a
temporary change. If you're taking
antibiotics, recovering from an illness,
or just finished a stretch of heavy
drinking, your liver enzymes and other
markers may not reflect your normal
baseline unless your doctor is checking
for exactly that reason. Second, testing
too soon after a medication change. If
you just started a new diabetes medicine
or adjusted your thyroid dose, give it
the time your doctor recommended.
Medications take weeks to show their
full effect, and early labs can mislead
you. And third, waiting until the last
minute. Some people get their blood work
done the day before an appointment or
cancel the visit because a few results
haven't arrived yet. But even partial
results can show something important,
like a sharp drop in kidney function or
signs of an infection that needs
treatment. So, get your labs done a few
days ahead and keep your appointment
even if some results are still pending.
Let's pull this together because it's
simpler than it sounds. Follow the
fasting instructions you were given and
drink water. Don't fast longer than you
were told. Ask about your medications
before the test, not after. Skip hard
workouts, heavy dinners, and alcohol.
Tell your doctor about every supplement,
specially biotin. Go at the time you
were given and let medication changes
settle before you recheck. And here's
the good news. You don't need to panic
over every small thing. A short walk
won't wreck your results. A normal
dinner is fine. And if no one told you
to fast, you probably don't need to.
What matters is following the
instructions for your specific test and
giving your care team the full story.
That gives your doctor numbers they can
trust, and it can save you extra pokes,
extra worry, and extra cost. Now, I'm
curious. Have you ever had a result come
back abnormal and then discovered it was
something you did beforehand? Tell me in
the comments. I read them, and your
story might help someone else avoid the
same surprise. If this video was useful,
share it with someone who has blood work
coming up soon. This video is for
educational purposes only and is not
medical advice. Always follow the
guidance of your own doctor. Thank you
for watching, and I'll see you in the
next one.

What Is the REAL Ideal Blood Pressure After 65? (It's Not What You Think)

Is blood pressure supposed to be higher after age 65? Is 140/90 considered hypertension in seniors? And what about 130/80—is that a normal blood pressure?

In this video, I explain what current blood pressure guidelines say about normal blood pressure after 65, why blood pressure often changes as we age, and the important difference between what is common in older adults and what is actually considered healthy.

We’ll also discuss systolic and diastolic blood pressure, isolated systolic hypertension, low diastolic pressure, orthostatic hypotension, and why your personal blood pressure target may depend on more than just your age.

65, is a reading of 135 over 85
something to worry about? Is 130 over 70
good enough? And can your blood pressure
really be too low just because you've
had a few more birthdays? These are
questions I get all the time, and the
honest answer is more personal than a
single number on a chart. Here's the
short version before we dig in. There is
no one target that fits every adult over
65. The right number depends on you, and
I'll show you exactly what that means in
a moment. In this video, I'll walk you
through what current guidelines say, why
blood pressure shifts as we age, when a
low reading deserves attention, which
hidden patterns can change the picture,
and what to ask your own healthcare
provider. Let's begin with a simple
idea, because it really is the heart of
this whole video. A blood pressure
reading can be typical for your age and
still not be ideal for your health.
Typical and healthy are two different
things. And on top of that, the goal a
provider sets for someone being treated
is not the same thing as the category a
reading falls into. Keep those two ideas
in your pocket, because the rest of the
video builds on them. So, what counts as
normal? For adults, normal blood
pressure is a top number under 120 and a
bottom number under 80. That cutoff
doesn't move when you turn 65 or 75 or
85. What moves is how many people land
above it. High readings become more
common with age, but common doesn't mean
it's where you want to be. If you're
watching this so far, hit subscribe now
and then tell me in the comments below,
what was your most recent blood pressure
reading? Top number and bottom number,
and where in the world are you watching
from? I read those comments myself, and
your answers show me exactly who I'm
making these videos for. Tap the like
button. It tells me you want more videos
like this one. Now, why do readings tend
to climb? It comes down to your
arteries. Think of a brand new elastic
band. Stretch it, let go, and it snaps
right back. Young arteries behave a lot
like that. With every heartbeat, the
walls give a little and spring back, and
that softens the push of the blood. Over
the years, arteries often become
stiffer. They give less, so each
heartbeat meets more resistance, and the
top number, the systolic pressure, is
usually the one that rises. That leads
to a pattern called isolated systolic
hypertension. The top number is high,
while the bottom number, the diastolic,
stays lower and is sometimes completely
normal. It's very common in older
adults, and it's linked to that
stiffening of the arteries, but please
don't hear this as harmless.
Being common doesn't make it fine. It's
still high blood pressure, and it's
something your health care provider will
want to look at and manage. There's a
related idea that many people have never
heard of, and it's the gap between your
two numbers. Subtract the bottom number
from the top number, and you get what's
called the pulse pressure. If your
reading is 140/70,
the gap is 70.
In younger adults with flexible
arteries, that gap tends to be narrower.
In older adults, a wide gap can be one
more sign that the arteries have lost
some of their cushioning. It's not
something to panic about, and it's not a
number you need to calculate every day,
but it's a good example of how a reading
holds more information than just high or
low, and it's a fair thing to ask your
provider about. Before we go further,
let me explain why I keep stressing the

stiff arteries to the same degree. Two
people can both be 72 and have very
different blood vessels, different
kidneys, and different daily lives. One
walks 3 miles a day, the other uses a
cane and takes six medications. It would
be strange to expect the exact same plan
to suit both. And that's the heart of
why this topic is more layered than it
looks. So, with all of that in mind,
what are doctors actually aiming for
when they treat blood pressure in an
older adult? The 2025 guideline from the
American Heart Association and the
American College of Cardiology sets a
general treatment goal of under 130/80
for adults with high blood pressure, and
that includes people over 65. Let me
slow down on one thing here. A category
describes where a reading falls. A
treatment goal describes where your
provider is trying to guide your
pressure once you're being treated.
They're connected, but they aren't the
same. And age on its own doesn't
automatically push the goal up to 140 or
150, even though many of us remember
hearing those numbers years ago. If
you're caring for a parent or a spouse,
or you're sorting this out for yourself,
and the numbers don't match what you
were told years back, tell me in the
comments what's confusing you. I read
them, and they help me decide what to
cover next. Now, let's turn the question

It can, but I want to be careful because
there isn't one danger number that fits
everybody. What matters is the reading
together with how you feel and your
overall health. Symptoms like dizziness,
light-headedness, weakness, fainting, or
unusual tiredness are worth bringing up.
This is also a good moment to talk about
the bottom number because so many people
only watch the top one. A diastolic
reading under about 60 is something a
provider may want to look at more
closely, especially in an older adult or
in someone with coronary artery disease.
Here's the reasoning in simple terms.
Your heart muscle receives much of its
own blood supply in the moments between
beats, when it relaxes. The bottom
number reflects the pressure available
during that rest. So, in someone whose
heart arteries are already narrowed, a
very low bottom number is something
worth looking at. That doesn't mean
every reading under 60 is a problem, or

heart or other organs. It means context
matters. Your provider will look at the
full picture, your symptoms, your

how your readings have behaved over

more situation I want every adult over

orthostatic hypotension. By definition,
it's a fall of at least 20 points in the
top number, or at least 10 points in the

standing. You may know the feeling, that
rush of light-headedness, that moment
when you need to steady yourself. But
feeling dizzy for a second doesn't
automatically mean you have it. The
diagnosis depends on actually measuring
the drop. In older adults, it can be
tied to certain medications, to not

how the body regulates pressure. That's
one more reason your symptoms matter,
and not only the number you get while
sitting still with a cuff on your arm.
Why does this matter so much? Because a
fall at this stage of life can change
things quickly. A broken hip, a hospital
stay, weeks of lost strength. Nobody
wants to trade a slightly better number

high pressure and risk a stroke, either.
Quick side note, because it comes up so

out is to measure it and talk about it.
Please don't just push through and say
nothing. Now I want to bring in one
study because it shapes so much of
today's thinking. It's called the SPRINT
trial. It enrolled roughly 9,000 adults
at higher risk for heart disease and
compared two systolic One group aimed
for under 120, and the other aimed for
under 140. The group with the lower goal
had fewer major cardiovascular events
and fewer deaths during the study. And
it wasn't only younger people. A large
share of participants were 75 or older,
and that older group also did better
with the intensive approach. There were
trade-offs. The intensive group had more
episodes of low blood pressure and more

other hand, among participants 75 and
older, the researchers did not find a

knowing that the trial left out people
with diabetes or a prior stroke. I won't
turn this into a full breakdown because
that isn't the point. The point is that
research like this nudged guidelines

reminding clinicians to look at the
person sitting in front of them. Let me
be fair to both sides of this
conversation because it's easy to hear
one half and miss the other. On one
side, the evidence for treating high

and many people live longer and
healthier lives because of it. If
someone told you that high pressure
after 65 is just a normal part of aging

accurate. On the other side, treatment
